title: US Senate Panel Advances Bill to Ban Chinese-Linked Vehicles From American Roads
excerpt: The bipartisan legislation would codify Biden-era restrictions on Chinese automakers while extending a ban to any company with more than 15% Chinese ownership — a provision that could also block Mercedes-Benz from the U.S. market.
body:
• The Senate Commerce Committee advanced a bipartisan bill that would ban vehicles, connected-car software, and hardware from companies with significant Chinese ownership from the U.S. market, starting January 1, 2027.
  • A provision barring automakers with more than 15% Chinese ownership could unintentionally block Mercedes-Benz, which has nearly 20% passive Chinese investment, from selling in the United States.
  • Committee Chair Ted Cruz warned the bill needs changes before passage, calling the ownership threshold a competitive weapon pushed by General Motors and the UAW against Mercedes-Benz.
  • All three Detroit automakers — GM, Ford, and Stellantis — along with the UAW support the legislation, which sponsors say addresses national security threats posed by data-collecting connected vehicles.

The U.S. Senate Commerce Committee on Wednesday advanced legislation that would significantly tighten restrictions on Chinese-linked automakers selling vehicles in the United States, codifying Biden-era rules while raising new questions about how broadly the ban might sweep.

The bill, introduced by Senators Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), would prohibit the import or sale of connected vehicles made or designed in China, North Korea, Russia, or Iran beginning January 1, 2027. It would also bar vehicles from any manufacturer with more than 15% ownership tied to entities in those countries.

Mercedes-Benz Caught in the Crossfire

That ownership threshold immediately drew sharp objections from Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who warned the provision would effectively ban Mercedes-Benz from the American market. The German automaker has nearly 20% passive Chinese investment and operates manufacturing plants in South Carolina and Alabama.

"We would never consider banning Mercedes-Benz sales in the United States."

— Senator Ted Cruz, Commerce Committee Chair

Cruz allowed the bill to advance without a formal roll call vote but said it would not pass the full Senate without amendments. He proposed letting the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) determine whether ownership stakes pose a risk, regardless of percentage. He also accused the UAW, which supports the legislation, of backing the 15% cutoff as retaliation for its failed campaign to unionize two Mercedes-Benz plants in Alabama.

Senator Moreno countered that Mercedes-Benz would have until 2030 to comply and could apply for Commerce Department waivers if needed.

National Security and Industrial Base

The sponsors framed the legislation as a defense of both national security and American manufacturing. Connected vehicles transmit data through cameras, satellite links, and cellular connections — capabilities the bill's backers say could be exploited by Beijing.

"Chinese cars are surveillance packages on wheels, with the ability to collect on American citizens and transmit that data back to Beijing."

— Senator Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan)

The bill would extend to connected-vehicle software by 2027 for companies with more than 25% ownership by covered countries, and to hardware — including semiconductor chips and onboard computer modules — by 2030.

All three Detroit automakers expressed support. General Motors said it "can compete with anyone in the world when we are given a level playing field." Ford said its leaders "look forward" to working with Congress on the measure. Stellantis called it a response to "important issues related to connected vehicle security and fair competition."

Production Already Shifting

Moreno cited concrete industry moves already underway. GM plans to shift production of its Chinese-made Buick Envision to the United States by the 2028 model year, and Ford has agreed to relocate Chinese-made Lincolns to American plants. Google's self-driving unit Waymo, which had been in discussions with Chinese automaker Geely about platforms, "has committed to looking at a Detroit-based manufacturer for their future platforms," Moreno said.

The broader supply-chain decoupling is intensifying. A Reuters report this week detailed how U.S. companies like Eagle Wireless, an Ohio-based electronics manufacturer, are racing to replace Chinese connectivity modules in American vehicles. Eagle expects to reach an annual run rate of 2 million modules by the end of Q3, though Chinese vendors still account for nearly half of global automotive cellular IoT module shipments, according to Counterpoint Research.

Polestar's Exit, Volvo's Survival

The legislation follows high-profile enforcement of existing rules. Last month, Polestar — majority-owned by China's Geely Holding — said the Trump administration was forcing it to stop selling vehicles in the United States beginning with the 2027 model year. Its sister brand Volvo, also owned by Geely, received authorization to continue U.S. sales by demonstrating compliant data-handling practices.

Ford has separately asked for authorization to continue importing some China-produced models. Cruz noted that GM was also pushing a separate provision requiring more expensive battery management systems, which he said would add about $5,000 to vehicle costs — a requirement he suggested was designed to benefit GM at competitors' expense.

What's Next

The bill now heads to the full Senate, where Cruz's concerns about the ownership threshold suggest amendments are likely before any floor vote. A similar bill is pending in the House of Representatives. The Commerce Department would retain waiver authority, with a 60-day congressional review period for any exemptions granted.

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, the legislation underscores the intensifying U.S.-China technology decoupling that is reshaping global automotive supply chains — dynamics that increasingly affect Indian auto-component suppliers who serve both markets and Indian-American professionals working across the industry.
